newsitem.title: USA: Soybean prices fall as U.S. crop flourishes.
newsitem.headline: Soybean prices fall as U.S. crop flourishes.

text.p: Soybean prices fell sharply on Monday, weakened by nearly ideal growing weather for newly planted crops in the United States and renewed prospects of imports from South America.

Forecasts called for showers across much of the U.S. Midwest, followed by warmer temperatures, meteorologists said. The forecast was a nearly ideal recipe for good crop development, floor sources said.

"The soycomplex is torn between a tight cash situation (lack of immediate supplies) and the prospects for a bumper, record crop," said John Kleist, director of agricultural research for ING Futures and Options in Chicago.
Prices had risen late last week on concern about a possible supply shortage in the U.S. before this year's crop is harvested.
But fears were eased slightly by signs that shipments from South America may help to alleviate any shortfall.
Brazilian traders said Monday that leading grain company Cargill Inc. was loading Brazilian soybeans destined for southern Georgia. Shipment was set for June 20.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery closed 16 cents a bushel lower at $8.38-1/2.
Wheat prices also fell sharply as rains boosted crop prospects in North Dakota, the leading wheat producing state in the U.S. for the last two years.

"Good rains over the weekend collapsed things," one wheat trader said, noting that before the showers there had been growing concern about dry weather in spring wheat growing areas in the northern Midwest.
"There are also some forecasts for rains later this week, so that (provided additional pressure)," he added.
Signs that a freeze earlier this year may have done less damage than many had feared to hard red winter wheat crops in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas also weighed on the market.
"Yields are better than expected in the freeze-damaged areas (of Oklahoma)," another wheat trader said.
Traders noted harvesting advanced rapidly over the weekend in southern Oklahoma.
Wheat for July delivery on the CBOT closed 9-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.42-3/4.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices remained rangebound in quiet trade Monday as players awaited fresh news on the renewal of Iraqi oil sales under its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations, traders said.
"The market went up and down hour-to-hour depending on (views of) the timing of Iraqi oil sales," said William Brown, an oil analyst and president of W.H. Brown & Co.
Crude oil for delivery in July ended 18 cents higher at $19.01 a barrel after a day of lackluster trade that saw it trade up to $19.18 and down to $18.77.
"It's my feeling that Iraqi oil sales will come later than the market tends to think," Brown added.
Prevailing views at the United Nations hold that the second round of oil sales, which officially began June 8, will likely begin in earnest by early July.
Iraq last week said it would not restart oil sales for the second phase of the oil-for-food accord until a new distribution plan for humanitarian aid was in place.
U.N. officials said it was up to Baghdad to complete a plan, then submit to the U.N. for final approval.
The oil-for-food plan is a humanitarian exception to broad sanctions the U.N. imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Traders said prices will edge higher the more the market becomes convinced of delays in the Iraqi oil sales.
Gasoline for delivery in July settled 0.63 cent higher at 58.03 cents a gallon, while heating oil for July delivery rose 0.30 cent to 51.94 cents a gallon.
